explanation: Complete transection of the spinal cord above C5 results in quadriplegia (paralysis of all four limbs) due to interruption of all descending motor pathways at the cervical level, along with respiratory compromise.

In spinal cord hemisection (Brown-Sequard), ipsilateral loss below lesion includes proprioception (dorsal columns) and upper motor neuron signs (corticospinal tract); pain/temperature loss is contralateral (spinothalamic decussation).
In Brown-Sequard syndrome, the LMN lesion at the level of lesion is ipsilateral (not contralateral); the lesion involves corticospinal tract (ipsi UMN signs) and dorsal columns (ipsi proprioception).
UMN lesion is characterized by spasticity (hypertonia), hyperreflexia, Babinski sign (plantar extension), and retained muscle bulk initially; option E (plantar flexion) describes normal reflex.
LMN lesion is characterized by flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, muscle wasting, fasciculations, decreased/absent reflexes, and no Babinski sign (plantar reflex absent or normal flexion).

Syringomyelia (fluid-filled cavity in central spinal cord) first affects crossing spinothalamic fibers in the anterior white commissure, causing bilateral loss of pain and temperature sensation in a cape-like distribution.

The hindbrain (rhombencephalon) includes medulla oblongata, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri is part of the midbrain (mesencephalon), containing cerebral peduncles with corticospinal tracts.
The brain stem consists of midbrain, pons, and medulla oblongata; the cerebellum is a distinct hindbrain derivative that overlies the fourth ventricle but is not part of the brain stem proper.
The cranial part of accessory nerve arises from nucleus ambiguus in the medulla (fibers that join vagus for laryngeal innervation); the spinal part arises from C1-C5 spinal cord levels.
The right spinal lemniscus carries crossed pain and temperature sensation from the left body (fibers have decussated at spinal cord levels before ascending in the spinothalamic tract).
The gracile and cuneate tracts are supplied by posterior spinal arteries and radicular arteries; the anterior spinal artery supplies the anterior 2/3 of the cord including corticospinal tracts.
Lumbar puncture is performed at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace (corresponding to below or above the L4 spinous process tip), which is well below the conus medullaris (L1-L2 in adults).

Complete cervical cord transection above C5 causes quadriplegia with loss of all motor function below the lesion, including respiratory muscles if the lesion is high enough to affect C3-C5 phrenic nerve origins.

In hemisection, ipsilateral findings below the level include proprioception loss (dorsal column) and UMN signs (corticospinal tract); contralateral findings are pain/temperature loss (spinothalamic decussation).

Brown-Sequard syndrome involves ipsilateral UMN signs below, ipsilateral proprioception loss below, and contralateral pain/temperature loss below; LMN signs at the level are ipsilateral, not contralateral.
UMN lesion features: spastic paralysis, hypertonia, hyperreflexia, Babinski positive; does NOT include hypotonia, marked wasting, or restricted paralysis (those are LMN features).
LMN lesion features: flaccid paralysis, hypotonia, muscle atrophy, fasciculations, absent reflexes; Babinski is NOT present (it's a UMN sign); hypertonia and increased reflexes are UMN features.
Syringomyelia first affects crossing spinothalamic fibers carrying pain and temperature (bilateral since fibers cross at multiple levels before forming the tract), creating a suspended sensory level.
The rhombencephalon (hindbrain) comprises the medulla, pons, cerebellum, and fourth ventricle; the crus cerebri belongs to the midbrain and contains corticospinal and corticopontine fibers.
Brain stem includes midbrain, pons, and medulla; it does NOT include cerebellum (though it connects to it via peduncles) nor the cerebral aqueduct (which is CSF space, not neural tissue).

The cranial accessory nerve fibers arise from nucleus ambiguus and travel with the vagus nerve to innervate pharyngeal and laryngeal muscles; this is why it is considered part of CN X's nerve pattern.
The spinothalamic tract crosses at or near the segmental level of entry and ascends as the spinal lemniscus carrying pain/temperature from the contralateral side of the body.

Dorsal column tracts (fasciculus gracilis and cuneatus) receive blood from posterior spinal arteries and radicular arteries that accompany dorsal roots; multiple sources prevent ischemia in most cases.
The L4 spinous process is the landmark for lumbar puncture; the needle is inserted at L3-L4 or L4-L5 interspace, below the level where the spinal cord ends (conus medullaris at L1-L2).
Transection above C5 causes quadriplegia (all four limbs) with potential respiratory failure if the lesion is very high; C3-C5 segments give rise to the phrenic nerve for diaphragm function.
In hemisection, ipsilateral loss includes dorsal column modalities (proprioception, vibration) and motor function (UMN signs below level); the same-level lesion also causes LMN signs ipsilaterally.
Brown-Sequard is ipsilateral motor/proprioception loss and contralateral pain/temperature loss below the lesion; at the level, there is ipsilateral LMN signs, not contralateral.
